entries.test: Oracle's financial disclosures and debt performance following an OpenAI payment failure would show whether its OpenAI exposure causes severe financial distress.
entries.note: The financial context gives 'fucked' a plain reading as severe financial trouble.
The proposition combines a measurable spending relationship with an explicitly very small probability of unspecified technological transformation.

entries.test: Semiconductor sales, orders and investment following the named companies' retreat from spending at least $30 billion quarterly would show whether the boom suffers a severe downturn.
entries.note: The normalization replaces the explicit $30 billion quarterly spending threshold with unspecified 'heavy' spending.

entries.test: Hyperscalers' Q3 2026 cash-flow statements, AI revenue disclosures and documented AI returns would test the spending crossover and claimed disclosure pattern.
entries.note: The Q3 2026 deadline has passed. The claim also includes a present causal explanation for limited revenue disclosure.

entries.test: Hyperscalers' new AI-related revenue through 2030 and the documented beneficiaries and uses of their AI infrastructure would test the $2 trillion threshold and fallback outcome.
entries.note: He asserts a necessary revenue threshold, rather than predicting that the threshold will be reached.

entries.test: Demonstrated recursive self-improvement or at least $600 billion in additional current-service revenue attributable to the specified GPU deployments would contradict the forecast.
entries.note: 'Digital God' is rhetorical, but the other predicted outcomes have testable content.

entries.test: GPU customer revenue breakdowns and the labs' payments relative to Google, Amazon and Microsoft cloud revenues would test exclusivity and the estimated 20% share.
entries.note: The source refers specifically to the H100, B200 and B300 deployments; the proposition broadens this to all hyperscaler GPUs.

entries.test: Public funding records and infrastructure expenditures attributable to supporting the two labs, excluding Oracle's Stargate buildout, would test the $500 billion estimate.
entries.note: The proposition drops 'I estimate,' although the separate conditions field records it. An attributed numerical estimate is still checkable.
'Effectively subsidiaries' describes dependence rather than legal ownership here. 'Complete waste of money' is an overall judgment of worth.

entries.test: Microsoft's AI revenue from customers and products other than OpenAI would show whether it has a substantial independent AI business.
entries.note: The surrounding revenue calculations give the exaggeration a concrete commercial reading.
'Likely' and 'I'd be surprised' explicitly hedge the claim. Expecting no dramatic change does not mean expecting the share to remain about 70%.
The proposition weakens 'only real outcome' to 'main outcome.' The source also explicitly qualifies its conclusion with 'appears to be.'

entries.test: Hyperscaler RPO disclosures and identified contracts with OpenAI and Anthropic would establish their dollar contribution and percentage of total RPOs.

entries.note: The central commitment is a judgment that further capital investment is irrational.

entries.test: Hyperscalers' AI revenue breakdowns excluding their investee labs would show whether substantial other AI revenues exist.
entries.note: The financial context supplies a plain reading of 'meaningful' as commercially substantial.

entries.test: Meta's published advertising experiments and revenue attribution analyses would show whether GPU-backed AI materially increases advertising revenue.
entries.note: The claim denies a causal contribution to revenue.

entries.test: The named suppliers' sales breakdowns, customer orders and hyperscaler capital spending would show whether speculative AI infrastructure investment accounts for their record sales.
entries.note: The proposition generalizes from five named companies to chip and memory sales overall and omits 'entirely.'

entries.test: AI data center contracts, utilization and customer spending would show whether demand exists beyond Anthropic and OpenAI.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion establishes that AI capacity is the relevant data center market.

entries.test: Customer compute spending, data center construction timelines and utilization after opening would test the claimed customer concentration and construction-delay explanation.
entries.note: 'Other' follows a list including Microsoft, NVIDIA, Google and Meta as well as the labs. Reducing that reference to 'besides the labs' is not faithful.

entries.test: Customer contracts and financing disclosures for the AI data center buildout would show whether paying customers exist beyond subsidized, unprofitable AI labs.
entries.note: 'Built for no-one' is qualified immediately by the exception for subsidized labs.
Calling spending wasteful and products bad expresses judgments of worth, even in insulting language.
The recommendation for an SEC investigation is normative. The embedded denial of $10 billion in attributable annualized revenue could be checked separately.

entries.test: Representative user sentiment, product revenue disclosures and GitHub Copilot's pricing, compute costs and adoption would test the reception, revenue and subsidy-dependence claims.
entries.note: 'Widely loathed' weakens 'near-universally loathed.' The proposition also asserts that subsidies caused Copilot's success.

entries.test: LLM reliability evaluations, operating costs and sustained deployments in deterministic automation would test the asserted technical and commercial unsuitability.
entries.note: 'Doomed' adds a broad prediction, but the reliability and automation claims have a plain empirical reading.
Rejecting something as proof does not deny that it is evidence. No shared empirical test establishes whether today's coding ability proves an unspecified future capability.
'Industry marketing' and 'questionable' are evaluative characterizations here. Specific allegations about omitted data or calculation methods would be separately checkable.

entries.test: The labs' revenue and compute spending for the relevant periods, compared with Exponential View's methodology and $110 billion total, would establish the claimed share.
entries.note: The source's displayed $44 billion and $20.25 billion subtotals sum to about 58.4% of $110 billion, rather than 68%.

entries.test: Amazon, Microsoft and Google's Q1 2026 depreciation disclosures would establish the amounts and whether their sum exceeds $25 billion.
entries.note: The printed figures sum to $33.44 billion; whether they are comparable to AI-only depreciation is a separate issue.
The alleged effect on retail investors is explicitly qualified with 'likely.'
The source alleges a private design intention. 'Even if you're not' allows real productivity, whereas 'a false sense' makes the feeling necessarily mistaken.

entries.test: Representative mental-health research among tech workers and evidence linking elevated illness to misleading AI capability claims would test the alleged epidemic and cause.
entries.note: Its inflammatory wording still makes an empirical claim about prevalence and causation.

entries.test: Public promises about autonomous AI work compared with reproducible product performance would show whether the promised capabilities are delivered.
entries.note: The preceding discussion identifies autonomous work and reduced human supervision as the relevant promises.
The source alleges a desire to frighten users, whereas the proposition presents fear-driven usage as an accomplished mechanism. The alleged private motive cannot itself be settled publicly.
Calling a tool a con evaluates its marketing and value. It does not precisely assert the proposition's technical definition of genuine autonomy.

entries.test: Working-hour and output measurements among workers subjected to the described AI adoption practices would test whether hours roughly double without greater output.
entries.note: The source addresses workers in an imposed workplace culture; the proposition broadens this to tech workers generally and attributes the effect directly to tools.

entries.test: AI companies' delivery against public commitments and eventual financing failures or sustained self-financing operations would test the claimed failure and capital exhaustion.
entries.note: The capital-exhaustion forecast has no deadline.
'Too big to fail' could mean guaranteed government rescue, systemic importance or commercial invulnerability. The passage does not specify which test applies.
Both source assertions are qualified as appearances. Not appearing to improve products with compute is different from appearing unconstrained by compute.

entries.test: Comparable task-level model and human costs, demonstrated worker replacement and provider margins would test the concrete cost, capability and profitability assertions.
entries.note: 'Nothing justifies the investment' weakens 'nothing is worth even a fraction' of it. That value judgment is separate from the checkable operational assertions.

entries.test: A documented slowdown followed by cessation of new-model training at either lab because of rising training costs would establish the forecast outcome.
entries.note: Rising training costs are the asserted cause, not a hypothetical antecedent.
The central dependence of open-model progress on frontier training is explicitly qualified with 'likely.'

entries.test: US oversight requirements, their documented origins and resulting delays to OpenAI and Anthropic model releases would test the prediction and causal explanation.
entries.note: Oversight is presented as an existing cause of future delays, not an uncertain antecedent.
'The jig is up' does not specify an observable fundraising outcome. The normalization supplies an analytical claim the quoted sentence does not clearly state.

entries.test: Public reporting or disclosures about SoftBank's attempted $6 billion loan and lenders' stated credit concerns would test the failed financing and its evidentiary basis.
entries.note: The loan failure is a firm factual assertion; 'suggests' marks the conclusion about bank confidence as an inference.

entries.test: Anthropic's financial results, $200 subscription allowances and equivalent token pricing would establish the losses and whether subscribers can consume $8,000 in token value monthly.
entries.note: Token value at published prices should not automatically be equated with Anthropic's underlying compute cost.
'Cost of intelligence' could refer to training expenditure, token prices, subscription costs or cost per successfully completed task. These measures can move in opposite directions.

entries.test: Contracts and utilization sufficient to support the discussed AI data center buildout, without the specified technological transformation, would contradict the demand claim.
entries.note: The same paragraph qualifies the claim as insufficient demand unless the technology changes dramatically. The normalization removes that condition and broadens 'these data centers' to AI data centers generally.

entries.test: Sustained paying demand sufficient to support the planned AI compute capacity without a major near-term technological transformation would contradict the claim.
entries.note: The demand condition is firm; only the possible price reduction is qualified with 'likely.' The extracted conditions field incorrectly makes cheaper pricing mandatory.

entries.test: The labs' compute contracts, growth-dependent financing, customer pricing complaints and contemporaneous valuation evidence would test the asserted commitments and market conditions.
entries.note: 'Market skepticism' dilutes the specific assertion that the market rejects a trillion-dollar valuation. Growth contingency need not mean a contractual cancellation clause.

entries.test: Market losses, defaults, bankruptcies and financial disruption when the AI investment era ends would show whether severe financial damage follows.
entries.note: 'I expect' expresses a firm expectation. 'When this era ends' supplies the stated antecedent.
